entities.name: Bank of Amsterdam
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Wisselbank Amsterdam (Amsterdam Exchange Bank) was founded in 1609 by the Amsterdam city government as the world's first modern central bank and a precursor of modern banking systems. The Bank of Amsterdam introduced currency stability to a Dutch Republic flooded with debased foreign coins, accepted deposits of commercial coins and issued standardized bank money ('bank guilders') at their full metal value — creating a reliable transaction medium for Amsterdam's global trade network.

The Bank of Amsterdam's innovation was profound: by maintaining strict reserve requirements and issuing bank money that traders trusted because it was fully backed by metal reserves, the bank created the prototype of a central bank's monetary function. Amsterdam's status as the world's financial center in the 17th century — its stock exchange (founded 1611) was the world's first permanent stock exchange, and its VOC (Dutch East India Company) the world's first publicly traded company — depended fundamentally on the Bank of Amsterdam's monetary stability.

The bank operated for 183 years until 1791, when it collapsed after the French-backed Batavian Republic took power. Its final decades saw declining standards: the bank had lent money to the VOC (in violation of its charter) and to the City of Amsterdam, departing from its reserve backing. The Bank of Amsterdam's model directly influenced the Bank of England (founded 1694) and the theoretical development of central banking, making it arguably the most historically important financial institution ever created despite its relatively small scale.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Bank of Amsterdam (1609) was the world's first modern central bank, whose reserve-backed currency innovation provided the monetary foundation for Amsterdam's 17th-century global financial supremacy and directly inspired the Bank of England — making it the founding institution of modern banking.
